newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Pulp prices seen falling now but up in Q4 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Pulp prices seen falling now but up in Q4 - analysts.

text.p: Pulp producers will not be able to push through price increases until year-end as world stocks are depleted slower than expected and a strong dollar caps upwards price pressure, analysts said on Friday.

Before the fourth quarter of 1997, when prices are expected to be above current levels, producers may even be forced to cut prices as production and inventory levels stay at levels that are simply too high, analysts say.
"I do believe we'll see at least one price increase in the fourth quarter, maybe $50," Handelsbanken forestry analyst Bjorn Danckwardt-Lilliestrom told Reuters.
Until then he saw prices at similar levels of $560 per tonne for softwood pulp, with a slight risk of downward pressure.
"It will be extremely hard to raise prices further in the short-run although the industry might try," he said.

Under the spotlight is Weyerhaeuser Co, the world's largest pulp producer, for any signals of an attempt to raise prices. Last week it said it hoped to boost prices by $50 a tonne in the second half of the year.

Earlier this month two Swedish companies, forestry cooperative Sodra and Stora AB, postponed planned pulp price increases to $610. Stora then said it hoped to be able to raise the softwood pulp price to $610 per tonne in February.
But analysts said falls were more likely.
"There's a great risk it will fall to $450 to $500 at the end of April," said Mads Asprem, Morgen Stanley analyst.
He forecast the level would hold through the summer and would rise in December to $500 or $550 per tonne.
"They are producing too much. There is too much inventory out there in the chain," Asprem said.

Analysts agree that the level of pulp inventories among North American and Scandinavian producers, or calculated as NorScan figures, are still a key barometer for the industry because of its regular monthly release.

The Norscan figures, which ran at just over 1.9 million tonnes in December which was unchanged on the previous month, must fall to 1.5 million tonnes in order for price increases to go through, analysts said.
London-based Paribas analyst Hubert de Marliave forecast the January figure at 2.05 million tonnes.
"In June 1996 it was slightly above 1.5 million and then it went sharply up. It really needs to stay below that level for a long time (in order for prices to increase)," de Marliave said.
"I think that it makes sense that it will decrease in the summertime, I think they usually do, and I expect them to be at 1.5 million in December 1997," he said.
Following consensus forecasts, de Marliave's pulp price estimates were $550 for the first quarter, $535 in the second, $560 in the third and $595 in the fourth.
To compound pulp producers' misery, analysts said a stronger dollar would further hinder pulp price increases and may force the price even lower.
"It's going to be harder to raise pulp prices in dollars as I see it," said Danckwardt-Lilliestrom.
"With a stronger dollar...European pulp producers will produce pulp at a lower dollar prices, so the risk for a larger fall in the pulp price is higher," Asprem said.
